deep.reconstruction:
Heading: 'Variae summationes serierum absconditae' ('various hidden summations of series'). Throughout, ϖ = 2.6220575543… is Gauss's lemniscate constant, the half-period of sin lemn, so ϖ/π = 0.8346268417…. The previous page carries the note 'ad 1799' and drafts addressed to the eighty-year-old Kästner (born 1719), so a date of about 1799–1800 is plausible. That is Gauss's lemniscatic period.

In modern notation 2/(e^x+e^{-x}) = sech x and 2/(e^x-e^{-x}) = csch x. The five stated identities are:

(1) Σ_{n≥1} sech²(nπ) = ϖ²/(2π²) + 1/(2π) − 1/2. Numerically both sides are 0.0074559.
(2) Σ_{n≥0} csch²((2n+1)π/2) = ϖ²/(2π²) − 1/(2π). Both sides are 0.1891455.
(3) Σ_{n≥1} csch²(nπ) = 1/6 − 1/(2π). Both sides are 0.0075117.
(4) Σ_{n≥0} sech²((2n+1)π/2) = 1/(2π). Both sides are 0.1591549.
(5) Σ_{n≥0} sech((2n+1)π/2) = ϖ/(2π). Both sides are 0.4173134.

These are the lemniscatic case of the q-series and Fourier expansions of elliptic functions: k = 1/√2, K = K', q = e^{−π} (so q^{1/2} = e^{−π/2}), and ϖ = √2·K(1/√2).
- (5) is the expansion cn u = (2π/(kK)) Σ q^{n+1/2}/(1+q^{2n+1}) cos((2n+1)πu/(2K)), evaluated at u = 0. This gives Σ sech((2n+1)πK'/(2K)) = kK/π = ϖ/(2π).
- (3) [my derivation]: with Q = e^{−2π}, csch²(nπ) = 4Σ_m m Q^{nm}. Hence the sum equals 4Σ_N σ(N)Q^N = (1 − E₂(i))/6. Since E₂(i) = 3/π, this gives 1/6 − 1/(2π).
- (1), (2) and (4) are the corresponding squared (dn²/cn²-type, E/K-dependent) expansions. ϖ² enters through K², and E is eliminated via Legendre's relation in the lemniscatic case.

Item '6)' is left empty.

Lower half: scratch work on the lemniscatic addition theorem. Write s = sl a, c = cl a, s' = sl b, c' = cl b. Gauss writes sl(a+b) = (cs' + sc')/(1 − scs'c'), his known form of the addition theorem. He then works on 1 + sl²(a+b):
- The denominator squared is 1 − 2scs'c' + sscc·s's'c'c'.
- The numerator squared is ccs's' + 2scs'c' + ssc'c'.
- Their sum is 1 + sscc·s's'c'c' + ccs's' + ssc'c', as written.

He uses the basic relation ccss + cc + ss = 1, i.e. cc = (1−ss)/(1+ss). It gives 1 − ss − cc = sscc, written also via 1 − 1/(ss+1) = ss/(ss+1). So the term 1 + sscc·s's'c'c' becomes 1 + (1−ss−cc)(1−s's'−c'c').

With t = 1 + ss one has ss = t−1, cc = (2−t)/t and 1−ss−cc = 2−t−cc. This yields the two further forms 1 + (2−t−cc)(2−t'−c'c') and 1 + (2−t)(t−1)(2−t')(t'−1)/(tt').

The last lines expand the full numerator, apparently aiming at a factorization: 1 + (1−ss−cc)(1−s's'−c'c') + ccs's' + ssc'c' = 2 − ss − cc − s's' − c'c' + sss's' + ccc'c' + 2ssc'c' + 2ccs's'. The calculation breaks off unfinished; my guess is that it aims at a closed form for 1 + sl²(a+b) or cl(a+b).
errors: No errors in the five summation formulas; all check numerically to at least 7 digits.
The algebraic scratch work is correct as far as it goes but is unfinished (the target factorization is not reached); one trial line '1+(t−1)' is struck out.
Item 6) is announced but left blank.

results.modern_name: Lambert/Eisenstein-series evaluation E₂(i) = 3/π (hyperbolic series at the lemniscatic point)
results.usually_credited_to: Follows from Jacobi's Fundamenta Nova (1829) expansions; often cited from Ramanujan's notebooks (Berndt)

results.modern_name: Fourier expansion of cn (and of cn²/dn²) at the lemniscatic modulus k = 1/√2

results.what: Σ sech²(nπ) = ϖ²/(2π²) + 1/(2π) − 1/2 and Σ csch²((2n+1)π/2) = ϖ²/(2π²) − 1/(2π)
results.modern_name: q-series for dn²/sn²-type sums (involving K² and E/K) at the lemniscatic point; quasi-modular E₂ evaluations
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi 1829; later Ramanujan-style hyperbolic series evaluations

results.what: sl(a+b) = (sl a·cl b + cl a·sl b)/(1 − sl a·cl a·sl b·cl b) and manipulations using s²+c²+s²c² = 1
results.modern_name: Addition theorem for the lemniscatic sine (Fagnano–Euler)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s); this form is Gauss's, known from his Nachlass (Werke III)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's lemniscatic-function work of 1797–1800, including Fourier/hyperbolic series for sl and cl that anticipate Jacobi, is well documented in Werke III/X. These summations are natural corollaries and are likely in or close to the published Nachlass. The neat closed forms involving ϖ² (equivalently E₂(i) = 3/π) are a nice detail but not historically startling.

transcription_corrections: The line read as 'ccss+cc+ss[?]' is the identity ccss + cc + ss = 1 (the final symbol is partly blotted).
Item 2° denominators should read e^{½π} − e^{−½π}, e^{3/2 π} − e^{−3/2 π}, e^{5/2 π} − e^{−5/2 π}; the transcription is essentially right.
'47c/31' at top right is struck through and replaced by the circled folio number (31).
'1+sscc s's'c'c'' should be read as 1 + ss·cc·s's'·c'c', i.e. 1 + s²c²s'²c'².

The scattered final lines are best read as: 1 + (1−ss−cc)(1−s's'−c'c') + ccs's' + ssc'c' = 2 − ss − cc − s's' − c'c' + sss's' + ccc'c' + 2ssc'c' + 2ccs's', with the side substitution 1−ss−cc = 2−t−cc, t = 1+ss.
